content: The Virupaksha Temple predates the Vijayanagara Empire and has remained in continuous worship; Krishnadevaraya added to it in the early sixteenth century.
The temple's eastern gopuram rises about 50 metres (around 160 feet) over the head of Hampi Bazaar and is visible from across the Sacred Centre.
Inside the temple, a small opening casts an inverted image of the main gopuram onto a wall, like a pinhole camera.

The stone chariot in the Vittala Temple courtyard is actually a shrine to Garuda built to look like a processional chariot; it is the best-known symbol of Hampi and appears on the Indian ₹50 banknote.
The Maha Mandapa of the Vittala Temple has slender pillars that give off musical tones when struck; tapping them is now prohibited to protect them.
The Vittala Temple dates from the fifteenth century and was greatly embellished during the reign of Krishnadevaraya.
Private vehicles stop at a car park and battery vehicles carry visitors to the temple; arriving at opening time avoids both heat and crowds.

The Lakshmi Narasimha statue was carved from a single boulder in 1528 during the reign of Krishnadevaraya and stands about 6.7 metres tall; the figure of Lakshmi that once sat on its lap was broken off.
The Badavilinga is a monolithic Shiva linga about 3 metres tall whose base always stands in water from an old irrigation channel.
Kadalekalu Ganesha is a monolithic Ganesha about 4.5 metres tall; the name refers to its belly resembling a Bengal gram (kadalekalu) seed.
Sasivekalu Ganesha is a monolithic statue about 2.4 metres tall; its name compares the belly to a mustard seed (sasivekalu).
The outer walls of the Hazara Rama Temple carry rows of carved processions of elephants, horses, dancers and soldiers, while the inner walls narrate the Ramayana in panels.
Located at the heart of the Royal Centre, the Hazara Rama Temple is believed to have been the private temple of the Vijayanagara royal family.
The Mahanavami Dibba is a tall stone platform from which the kings watched the nine-day Mahanavami (Dasara) celebrations; its sides are carved with hunting, dancing and procession scenes.
The Stepped Tank was uncovered during excavations in the 1980s; its precisely cut stone blocks carry mason's marks that helped in reassembly.
The Queen's Bath has a plain exterior but an ornate interior corridor of arches and balconies around a large bathing pool, once fed by an aqueduct.
The Lotus Mahal is named for its lotus-bud shaped arches; it combines Hindu tiered roofs with Indo-Islamic arches and is thought to have been a pleasure pavilion for the royal women.
The Elephant Stables have eleven tall chambers, each with a different domed roof, arranged symmetrically around a central pavilion.
Matanga Hill is the highest point in central Hampi and is best known for sunrise; the climb is steep and rocky and should not be attempted in the dark or alone.
In the Ramayana tradition, Matanga Hill is where the sage Matanga lived and where Sugriva took refuge from his brother Vali.
The Achyutaraya Temple was built in 1534, during the reign of Achyuta Deva Raya, and is dedicated to Tiruvengalanatha, a form of Vishnu.
The Sule Bazaar leading to the Achyutaraya Temple is one of Hampi's quietest ruins and is often nearly empty in the early morning.
Coracles are round boats of woven bamboo made watertight with a covering; rides are suspended when the Tungabhadra is running high, typically during and after the monsoon.
By tradition the King's Balance was used on special occasions to weigh the king against grain, gold or jewels, which were then distributed to priests and the poor.
The ASI museum at Kamalapura displays sculptures, coins and weapons recovered from Hampi and has a large scale model of the ruins; it is closed on Fridays.
Anegundi was a fortified settlement before Vijayanagara rose across the river and is often described as the older capital of the region.
Anegundi is known for community craft work such as banana-fibre and grass products, and for traditional homes that are still lived in.
Anjanadri Hill is revered as the birthplace of Hanuman; the temple on its summit is reached by climbing several hundred steps.
Sanapur Lake is a reservoir surrounded by boulder hills; swimming is dangerous because of deep water and hidden rocks.
Hemakuta Hill holds some of Hampi's earliest temples, which predate the Vijayanagara period, and is one of the most popular sunset viewpoints.
The Krishna Temple was built by Krishnadevaraya in 1513 to celebrate a military campaign in Odisha; its idol of the child Krishna is now in a museum in Chennai.
The Underground Shiva Temple lies several metres below ground level, and its inner sanctum is often flooded, so expect wet stone and some steps.
Pampa Sarovar is one of the lakes considered sacred in Hindu tradition and is linked in the Ramayana to Shabari's meeting with Rama.
